newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia set to become sugar exporter this year.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia set to become sugar exporter this year.

text.p: Ethiopia, reputed to be the original source of coffee, will become a sugar exporter when its fourth sugar factory opens mid this year, senior government officials said on Thursday.
They said the $226 million Finchaa Sugar Factory, built in western Ethiopia, would be operational in July. The Finchaa facility has an annual output of some 100,000 tonnes.
Finchaa is financed through loans from the African Development Bank (AfDB), Australia, Sweden, Spain and the Ethiopian government, according to government documents.

In addition to sugar, Finchaa factory will produce for export up to eight million litres of ethanol alcohol a year -- a by-product which could be mixed with petrol and used in motor vehicles, Finchaa officials told Reuters.

Ethiopia's three sugar estates of Wonji, Shoa and Metehara - - established in the 1950s during the rule of the late Emperor Haile Selassie as joint ventures with a Dutch company -- produce a total of nearly 220,000 tonnes of sugar annually to meet local demand, according government figures.
The three sugar estates were nationalised under the Marxist regime of ousted dictator Mengistu Haile Mariam and remain state property even now.

The government says the establishment of Finchaa factory in an area hitherto untouched by major projects will help to open up the region to infrastractural development such as roads, schools, hospitals, and potable water services.
The factory will also provide employment opportunities to around 5,000 people in the region, government officials added.
Sugar was introduced in Ethiopia during the five-year Italian occupation in the 1940s. Before that, Ethiopians drank sugarless coffee or even spiced it with a pinch of salt.

Ethiopia plans to ease dependency on coffee and has put on its agenda exporting tea as a priority. It sees the Finchaa factory as a major breakthrough in development of a sector long undermined by low investment.

This Horn of African country produced up to 3,500 tonnes of tea in 1995/96 but failed in export efforts because prices in the international market were very weak, according to officials at the state Tea Production and Marketing Enterprise.
The tea was sold locally and saved $25 million Ethiopia would have spent on tea imports, they say, adding that tea production was likely to rise in 1996/97.
The Ethiopian government owns two tea estates with 2,044 hectares (5,047 acres) in the west of the country.
Coffee remains Ethiopia's main cash crop and brings in about 60 percent of its hard currency.
